units.title: The Concept of Development
units.intro:
Development is not only GDP. It is whether people live longer, learn, work decently, and keep the environment that feeds them. Indicators: income, literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, access to water, energy use. HDI-style thinking mixes income + health + school even if the letters HDI are later.

Simple split: more economically developed / less — but it is a line, not two boxes. Development can be uneven inside one country (capital vs periphery). Sustainable development: meet today without wrecking tomorrow’s soil, water and climate (Unit 1–2 coming back).

cards.title: 4.1.1 Causes of Underdevelopment
body: Less developed countries have been trying to improve their economic conditions and they followed various development strategies.
In some countries, income of the population has declined.
Three reasons are often given to explain underdevelopment.
The first reason is lack of sufficient natural resources.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Requirements for Development
body: **Development** is an internal process, and different countries can follow different paths to reach an advanced level.
Every underdeveloped country should identify a long-term stable path that is compatible with its specific conditions.
For development to start as an internal process, certain conditions need to be fulfilled.
Access to resources is one of the fundamental requirements for development.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is the most widely used economic measure of development globally?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify key economic indicators.**
Development is measured by economic indicators (per capita income, energy use, employment structure) and social ones (literacy, nutrition, health).

**Step 2: Identify the most common.**
Per capita income is a widely used economic measure of development.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Per capita income**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to Malthusian theory, population tends to grow in:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review Malthus's population growth theory.**
Malthus analyzed population and food growth rates.

**Step 2: Identify population growth progression.**
He concluded that population tends to grow at geometric progression ($$2, 4, 8, 16...$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct option is **Geometric progression**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A resource management method based on replacing a non-renewable or scarce resource with an alternative renewable one is known as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review resource management methods.**
- Substitution: one type of resource replaces a non-renewable one.
- Recycling: resources are used over and over again.

**Step 2: Match the definition of replacement.**
This is known as substitution.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct option is **Substitution**.

cards.title: 4.2 Economic Measures of Development
body: Different experts have developed different measures.
Non-economic indicators, also called social indicators, reflect individual or group well-being.
The proportion of population with access to safe drinking water, levels of literacy, number of medical doctors per 10,000 people, and more. are some examples of non-economic indicators.
**Per capita income** is a widely used economic measure of development.

cards.title: Tip
body: Never use only money. Pair a cash indicator with a human one (literacy or child deaths) and one environmental caution.

cards.title: How to argue “developed” on paper
body: Pick three unlike indicators: one money (GNI or GDP per person), one body (life expectancy or infant mortality), one mind (years of school or literacy). Then add one limit: inequality (averages hide a slum next to a tower) or environment (income from mining that strips a slope).

Sectors: a farm country can still be “developing” if most people are in primary work with low yield. Factories (secondary) raise output but need power and skills. Services (tertiary) dominate rich-city job lists. Skipping straight to services without food and power is a shaky ladder.

Sustainable development in this syllabus is concrete: terrace so next year’s soil exists; manage grazing so the range is not a dust patch; use woodlots so the last highland tree is not the school stove. It is Unit 2 wearing a policy hat.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The less developed countries are structurally characterized by having a:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check less developed country characteristics.**
Less developed countries are characterized by low income, technological backwardness, and dominance of primary production.

**Step 2: Match with employment structure.**
This matches having a large proportion of the farming (agricultural) population.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Large proportion of farming population**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is classified as a non-renewable or fund resource?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources.**
- Renewable: crops, water, wind, solar.
- Non-renewable: gold, oil, copper.

**Step 2: Select the non-renewable option.**
Copper is a non-renewable (fund) resource.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Copper**.

glossary.meaning: Per capita income is a widely used economic measure of development.
Development is a dynamic and cumulative process.
Education is the major driving force for development.
Poverty is a prevalent condition in almost all less developed countries.

tips.text: Countries of the world are divided into the developed and underdeveloped ones on the basis of the level of development they have attained.
Most of the developed countries are in the northern hemisphere, while most of the less developed countries are in the southern hemisphere.
Development implies the well-being of people. It brings about qualitative change in the lives of people.
Improving the well-being of people is the desire and mission of every good government. However, due to numerous problems and obstacles, many countries remain underdeveloped.
Africa as a whole is the least developed continent.
Poverty, hunger, diseases, internal conflicts and violence are some of the factors that push many Africans to migrate to the developed countries.
Many African countries have rich natural resources, but they remain poor due to mismanagement and corruption.
